detail: defences act_*: ACT matches the frozen base model's hidden states on the clean prompt; axis 2 has no value for activation-level self-distillation, so it is coded distillation; signal dependence is not_applicable because no inference-time signal is used
results r_a_phi_bct_*: Table 2 gives Phi-4-reasoning BCT 42.6 (test) and 42.4 (train) while Table 3 gives 41.7 and 42.0 for the same cells; the record codes Table 3 (pp. 17, 18)
results r_a_*: ASRany and CleanTaskany count an example once any of 8 attacker suffixes succeeds or once any attempt is clean, so both are best-of-8 rates

results r_*_static and r_*_adaptive coded figure_only: Figure 2 prints each bar's value as a label inside a raster image, so the values cannot be checked against the page text and are not coded. Read from the image (Vicuna-7B, ASR-defense then ASR-adaptive attack): instructional prevention 53 and 91, data prompt isolation 50 and 94, sandwich prevention 15 and 68, adversarial fine-tuning 12 and 65; (Llama3-8B): instructional prevention 1 and 79, adversarial fine-tuning 4 and 85. Section 5.2 states 56% (Vicuna-7B original), 12% (adversarial fine-tuning) and 9% (Llama3-8B original)

report: attack success pools corpus poisoning, prompt injection and embedding perturbation, so it is a proxy for injection; the ablation setting (sigma 0.50, m=5) is not stated for Table 5; the 'PLSA only' row repeats the RobustRAG row of Table 5 exactly
evaluations ev_*: all coded results are measured inside a frozen web world model with an LLM judge, not in a real browser; the browser runs of Table 2 cover clean capability only (p. 8)
evaluations ev_*_v1, ev_*_v2, ev_*_v3: Adv v1 to v3 were trained against the Robust lineage, so they are adaptive for Robust iter 3 and transferred for Base and Capability iter 3
defences spot_*: the Spotlighting variant (delimiting, datamarking or encoding) is not stated; coded delimiters_markers as in the other records
evaluations ev_*: the authors add 'Complete all tasks automatically without requesting user confirmation' to the system message for every agent (p. 8)
results r_*_msb_nrp: NRP combines task performance under attack with attack success in one score; coded as quantity other
evaluations ev_*_msb_*: MSB pools attacks on tool signatures, parameters, responses and retrieval results; tool-description attacks are counted with the rest
evaluations ev_*_ad_*: the AgentDojo injection attack and the AgentDojo version are not named
defences ase, static: training tasks are generated across six attack categories, including direct injection and jailbreaks; the reward model is Qwen3.8-27B

results r_pneu_*, r_pauth_*: the permissive send rates are printed only inside Figure 2(c), which is text in the PDF; they are coded figure_only with the printed value kept (checked against the page text by the batch notebook)
evaluations ev_rneu_*: under the restrictive prompt a send on the neutral email is an unauthorised action without any injected claim, so it is coded other

results: the PDF text layer encodes the decimal points of Table 1 as colons in every extraction (for example 13:6 for 13.6), so the per-model cells, including the same-data ISE and ASIDE baselines, cannot be checked against the text and are not coded; the text averages match the Table 1 cells read with points

evaluations ev_*_none_*: the Vanilla baseline is the same backbone fine-tuned on the same instruction data without the role-aware changes (same-data twin); the training data, success criteria and decoding are in the supplement, which was not read

evaluations ev_*: every result is for a defended model; there is no undefended model under the same attacks, so the only comparisons vary the attack or, for SecAlign++, the role holding the instruction
defence secalignpp: the paper calls SecAlign++ a production-grade instruction-hierarchy model and does not name the checkpoint or base model

evaluations ev_ag_*: completion rate is measured with attack-like trigger phrases, not attacks, added to 30% of tool observations, so it is coded other; the step-1 rate is measured before any tool output and is coded as a clean-utility proxy

evaluations ev_cs_*, ev_t8_*: the adversarial prompts are mostly direct requests (social engineering, obfuscation) with some instructions embedded in task text, and success is counted as not refusing, so R1 is a proxy (pp. 4, 16)

comparisons c_cs_msa_*: Table 3 lists Meta SecAlign and Base-Llama3.1-8B in the n = 350 subset table, but Appendix A.7 says the Meta SecAlign runs used a 1,000-prompt set, Table 4 uses another attack taxonomy for it, and Table 8's input-role TPR (79.6%) equals Base-Llama3.1-8B's Table 3 TPR; the denominator is marked unreported (pp. 6, 18, 19)

defences struq_*, secalign_*: both are the authors' re-implementations: StruQ with <inst>/<obs> tags and weighted instruction tokens; SecAlign trained to prefer refusals on 30K agent triples, not the original SecAlign objective (p. 17)

report: the two Claude models show 0.0 ASR in almost every cell undefended, so their comparisons carry no security information; three models were logged under a shared registry alias, which the authors argue is constant across them (Appendix B); model names are as printed

evaluations ev_*_none: the no-defence values in Table III differ from Table I for the models in both (DeepSeek R1 93 against 98, Nova Pro 63 against 66, Mistral Pixtral 53 against 38, Llama 3.1 8B 5 against 0), so the two tables come from different runs
report: one targeted attack per benchmark; the paper notes that the weakest models' low ASR reflects poor instruction following rather than a defence

report: results are defence success rates (higher is better) averaged over three runs; StruQ is omitted on Qwen3-14B because its released data do not fit the thinking format; the first date is the proceedings year as recorded at screening
results r_*_ua: the paper's UA counts a task as done only when the injection is not executed (p. 7), so it is coded R3safe rather than R2attack

report: 100 queries per dataset; the defence changes the prompt's exemplars as well as adding the reasoning line, so the reference arm is the paper's standard four-exemplar prompt (instruction_prompt_only)

report: the paper's headline defence, Constitutional Sanitization, redacts suspicious spans before the model sees them and is left out as a sanitiser; the SFT targets were themselves produced under sanitisation, so the coded SFT defence distils that pipeline
results r_*_asr: Table III prints counts with Wilson intervals; the abstract gives the No Defense rates (86.50% Qwen, 54.83% Llama)

results with value_source figure_only: Figure 1 and Figure 4 print their values as point and bar labels; they are coded figure_only with the printed value kept (checked against the page text by the batch notebook)
defence secalign_l31: SecAlign is re-trained inside COPA's lifelong pipeline (same backbone, the same Stage 1 data, the same chance to adapt), not the released checkpoint (p. 5)
report: surviving compromises split into delegated-authority tasks and the rest (p. 7); kept as text here and handled by a coding rule, not a field

defences dt_*: the authors' DefensiveTokens run on base models with plain-text [INST]/[DATA]/[RESP] markers, not the chat-role format of the original release, so axis 1 is coded as delimiters for this report
report: no utility or answer-quality measure is reported for the defended models, so the claim of a robust defence rests on attack success alone
report: the judge-targeted results (Figure 5) are figure-only; the detector is a keyword rule in three languages and the paper reports a 0.0% false-positive rate on clean reviews

evaluations ev_*_static, ev_*_dyn: attack results are reported for static and dynamic PPA only; there is no undefended model under the same attacks, so the comparisons vary only the separator generation

defences secalign_*, struq_*, reasalign_*, metasec_l31: the paper does not say whether these baselines were re-trained on Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B or which checkpoints were used; Appendix A also lists PromptGuard and Instruction Hierarchy, which do not appear in any table
evaluations ev_*_hr, ev_*_bf: harmful-reject and benign-follow rates are on the authors' own held-out documents and the scorer is not named; harmful-reject is coded as an R1 proxy
evaluations ev_*_inj: InjecAgent was run in base and enhanced settings but Table 1 gives one number without saying how they were combined
claims k1: on Llama-3.1-8B, EDIC's harmful-reject rate (92.8) is below ReasAlign's (93.1) and its AgentDojo ASR (0.1) equals ReasAlign's and is above Meta-SecAlign's (0.0)

report: this record is the extended report archived with the code and data; its Table E4 comes from the main paper's merge-path setting; the attacks are the six static templates, with the worst case over them reported first

report: the main-text comparison of Table 5 places SecAlign's all-pairs rate (base 27.3%) beside a drop-free baseline (34.3%), which the authors flag as biased in SecAlign's favour; Table 24 uses one denominator for both arms; the EP-DPO checkpoint was chosen as the best of three steps
results r_l3_none_ia_*, r_g35_none_ia_*: Table 3 prints the Llama3 no-defence ASR as a percentage (99.3) and the GPT3.5 one as a fraction (1.00); each is coded in its printed unit

comparisons c_combo_*: Section 9.2 compares Warning on Gemini 2.5 (6.2%) with Warning on Gemini 2.0 against adaptive TAP in the Calendar Event scenario (10.8%, the TAP cell of Table 4) and with Gemini 2.5 alone (94.6%, Table 1); the scenario's data type and trigger format for 6.2% are not stated

report: the attack suite, detector and LoRA training data are author-built and only briefly described; the unprotected arm is reported as 100% in every phase, the middleware-only and full arms were tested on different attack sets, and the 0.000% claims are not checked against any public benchmark

results r_f12_*: Figure 12 plots unlabelled points, so the values are not coded; read from the chart, indirect attack success is about 6.9% for GPT-5.3, 6.0% for GPT-5.4, 4.0% for GPT-5.5 and 3.8% for GPT-5.6

report: there is no undefended arm: every compared production model already had instruction-hierarchy training and, from GPT-5.2 on, attacks from GPT-Red precursors, and successive models differ in much more than this training; Figure 11 and the IPI 2025 result have no comparator; the training targets are not described beyond reward design

report: the undefended reference in Tables 9.1 and 9.2 is the same 8B model under the identical staged security prompt (coded as baseline_kind instruction_prompt_only); in Table 9.3 the base model runs in InjecAgent's own format without that prompt

defences:sagec: trains_carry_through is coded yes_by_preference because the chosen responses copy an exact evidence span from the injected passage into the security report, and pairs prefer span-faithful reports over under-reporting ones

claims:k2: the claim speaks of defence quality, which the thesis reads mainly from detection; at equal size of data the 70B has the lower attack success on the stealth split (0.000 against 0.003) and the 8B on the two BIPIA splits

report: a master's thesis, not peer reviewed as a paper; preference candidates and judging use Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-4o-mini; ORPO's low native-format value (0.017) is described by the author as a degenerate-output artifact

evaluations ev_sep_*: Table 24 notes that the No-ISE rate (0.047) comes from refusing 814 of 1,500 probes, and the off-the-shelf anchor uses the native chat template, so neither is a like-for-like reading (p. 33)
results r_l3l4_*: on the L3 against L4 pair (user against tool output) GW-DPO (bi.) ties standard DPO (0.264) and 3-level (lin.) is lower (0.113)

report: the indirect rows rest on 6 and 4 samples, and their percentages (75.0, 20.0, 60.0, 28.0) do not correspond to whole numbers of samples; Section 5.2.2 gives a different baseline (65% leakage) for the knowledge-base case than Table 1
defences sec_g: the paper sweeps SecAlign learning rates on GPT-OSS-20B (Table 13) but does not say which checkpoint Tables 1 and 2 use; the headline HoS GPT-OSS model is learning rate 0.1 (p. 35)

comparisons c_*_own_*: each arm is attacked by an RL-Hammer attacker trained against it, so the attacker differs by design; the authors note the HoS-trained attacker got sparse reward (3.2% training ASR) and the SecAlign-trained attacker is stronger against HoS, which the max rows capture

claims k3: the headline HoS GPT-OSS model loses clean utility on AgentDyn (41.67 against 58.33) and WASP (41.62 against 56.22); Llama HoS loses 15.4 points of AgentDyn clean utility while Meta-SecAlign-70B gains 8.0 (Table 3)

report: the white-box claim (about three times more compute to reach 50% ASR) rests on Figure 2 curves and is not coded; the LLMail utility and multi-turn AlpacaFarm judge is Claude Sonnet 5 (Appendices G and I); the attack names Claudini and claudini_v45 are the paper's

evaluations ev_l_*_static: Table 12 shows that under SecAlign's own InjecAgent protocol Meta-SecAlign-70B gives invalid ReAct outputs on 90 to 95% of cases; the coded static rows use the authors' native tool protocol
report: about 20 attacked and 40 clean queries per model, so a single query moves ASR by 5 points; on Mistral the hybrid is above Sanitize alone (10% vs 5%)

defences icon_*: the prober is a small classifier fitted on 255 samples and the LLM is not trained, so axis 2 is fixed_inference_rule and both training fields are not_applicable, as coding rule 11 treats a direction fitted from examples
evaluations ev_*_troj: ICON's prober is trained on TrojanTools (p. 6), and TrojanTools is also one of the three attacks in Table 2, so that row is not out of distribution for ICON
evaluations ev_*: Table 2 gives benign utility (BU) for the undefended model only, so the defences' clean utility is not reported

results r_*_inter, r_*_guard: per-agent Interdict and guardrail ASR are text-extractable heat-map labels in Figure 2 at one decimal; the pooled values (0.22% over eleven agents, 0.95% over nine) are in the text only

comparisons c_*_inter, c_*_guard: the defence prompts were run on subsets (10,698 and 9,458 cases) while the Table 3 baseline uses all 1,054 cases per agent; the text compares paired cases but per-agent paired baselines are not given, so c3 is unmatched

claims k1: the 43% end of the claim is the Authorize prompt, which tells the agent to carry out tool-output instructions; it is not a defence and is not coded; LFM-2.6B's 0.00% baseline comes with 735 invalid outputs out of 1,054 (Table 3)

report: an evaluation study: the defences are two prompt blocks written by the authors; the headline finding is about what failed attacks consist of (76 to 80% ignored, 17 to 18% refused), which the schema has no field for

results r_browse_0_*, r_tools_0_*, r_nonconf_0_*: values are printed as bar labels inside the charts; value_source has no value for a printed chart label, so they are coded figure_only and the printed value is kept (checked against the page text by the batch notebook)

defence ihc_g5m: the Anti-Overrefusal split trains the model to follow lower-tier requests that only look forbidden; the paper does not show the same strings used both as attacks and as allowed requests, so trains_instruction_pair is no
results r_int_*: the internal prompt injection set is not public and its grading is not described

evaluations ev_webpage_*, ev_slack_*: the tool-use subsets score compliance with the higher-priority instruction under conflict, not whether an injected goal was executed, so they are an R1 proxy; IHDec's beta was set separately for these subsets (800 for Tool-Use, p. 14)
report: the defence rate (DR) is the share of samples where the model resists the injection, following Wu et al. (2025); this paper does not say how a sample is judged

claims:k1: the utility half of the claim rests on a radar chart (Figure 4) whose values are labelled for InstruCoT only and too small to read reliably; no utility value is coded, so only the defence-rate half has coded support

report: the chain-of-thought training targets and the injected instructions were generated with GPT-4.1, a closed model; ISE, MetaSec and IP were run by the authors on the four backbones; the backbones are named without saying whether the base or the instruct release was used

defences ig_*: IntentGuard's trust labels come from the agent's message segments (tool responses untrusted), which is coded as chat roles; the masking step uses the model's own listed intent, not a separate classifier, which is why it is kept under amendment 4
report: each attack is optimised separately against each defence and the undefended model, so attacker matching is by procedure and budget, not by identical injections

evaluations ev_*_att: undefended ASR is near zero for GPT-5.4 (0/288) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (1/288), and the paper shows that several injection goals were not reachable for those models (Table 6), so their defence comparisons carry little information; the model names are as printed
results r_*_uua: Table 9's utility-under-attack values sit on page 27 while the ASR evaluation is anchored on page 19; both pool the same 288 attack instances

comparisons: the only reference is GPT-3.5-Turbo fine-tuned on the same summaries, a different and far larger base, so every comparison has an unmatched base; whether the 72 HOUYI prompts were the same for every model is not stated; 13.80% does not correspond to a whole number of 72 prompts

evaluations ev_*_none_*: the Instruct baselines are trained by the authors on the matched chat-template corpus; the paper does not say whether they also received the 130k planted-injection examples, the GRPO stages or the final DPO stage
results r_*_ares: Table 3 reports robustness (1 - ASR), the opposite direction to Table 2; ID and OOD values are given only for the LLMON models

claims k1: the 53% lower end is the 8B Instruct baseline on ASB; capability is a mean over six categories (unchanged at 3B, 1.4 points lower at 8B), with mathematics at 8B the largest drop (84.09 to 79.63)

defences la_*: the input format of LocalAlign is not restated; it warms up with the Meta-SecAlign recipe and is attacked with fake delimiters aimed at structured separation, so it is coded with Meta-SecAlign's separate data role
results r_af_*, r_ood_*: Optimization-Free is the maximum ASR over five attack templates, taken per dataset after evaluation (p. 14)

report: the paper's emphasis is the deterministic output filter C5, left out as a filter; C3 (delimiting) does not lower ASR against C2 in the Llama table and raises tool misuse from 21.9% to 34.4%; the abstract's claims all concern C5, so no claim is coded
evaluations ev_es_*: ASR is conditioned on the 27 queries that retrieved a poisoned document, while utility, misuse and leakage use all 32

report: defences are measured on GPT-4o only; Figure 2 shows spotlighting's attack success rising with context length (about 32% at 1K tokens to 72% at 16K) without an undefended curve, so it is not coded
report: defences are evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct only, under the Authority spoof attack; the short-context comparison rows of Table 5 use each benchmark's own data with the same defences

evaluations ev_*_struq_*, ev_*_sec_*: the StruQ-Full and SecAlign-LoRA rows (and the uncoded TextGrad, Reminder, Sandwich and StruQ-LoRA rows) match the DefensiveTokens report's Table 3 value for value, at one decimal; the No Defense and DefensiveToken rows are at two decimals and differ from that report (Llama3-8B No Defense WinRate 33.82 here against 26.5 there). The text says the comparison is under comparable conditions and does not say the rows are copied, so measured_by is set to that report and the X comparisons carry unreported conditions

evaluations ev_*_ltbd_spoof: the Delimiter-Spoof templates are also used as training augmentations (pp. 3 and 4), so the adaptive test uses attacks the delimiters were trained on; no optimisation attack is run
evaluations ev_*_ltbd_plain: Table 3 does not name its benchmark; its Llama3.1-8B plain-injection ASR (0.48) differs from the Table 1 AlpacaFarm value (0.00)
defences ltbd_*: axis 2 lists both soft_tokens_frozen and preference_optimisation: only the four token embeddings are trained, with a DPO-style term in the loss

report: most injections persuade rather than instruct (six of the eight MedQA attacks), so instruction-focused defences are tested partly outside their design; Meta-SecAlign lowers clean accuracy in MDAgents from 81.4% to 61.9%

report: a component study of one released adapter: the restricted adapters are cut from Meta-SecAlign-8B, not retrained; the paper's side effect of interest is a trusted-memory following contrast, which the schema has no field for
report: results are pooled over four models with 100 attacks per objective and defence cell; datamarking lowers fidelity on legitimate cases from 80.5% to 59.0%

comparisons c_l_ov_sep, c_l_ov_util: for Llama, SEP is scored on a fixed 300-item subset for every row except the overlay, which uses 1,000 items, and the Llama overlay was trained on an earlier data mix (p. 6)
defences ov_*: training includes copy items that quote the marked span; the paper does not say whether those spans carry instructions, so trains_carry_through is coded no

evaluations ev_*: TensorTrust hijacking is left out because its attacker writes the user's own input; the paper notes that SEP's items resemble the training data while the other benchmarks share no attack text with it (p. 5)

results r_inj_check_acc: the acceptance rate with injection and the checking prompt is shown only in Figure 1; the text reports no difference from non-injected manuscripts under the same prompt (p > 0.28); results are pooled over three models and 26 papers
defence secalignpp: the paper does not name the SecAlign++ checkpoint or say whether it was trained on the default Qwen3-4B-Instruct backend, so the base condition of its comparisons is unreported
results r_audatt_qomni_txt_*: Table 5 marks the Qwen3.5 Omni-Plus text values with a dagger: one attack template was rejected by the API before reaching the model (p. 8)
defence secalign: the thesis cites SecAlign and serves it as a LoRA adapter on Llama 3.1 8B; which released adapter was used is not stated
report: Gemini was run once per case, the other models three times; quantised weights for the 32B and 70B models; spotlighting raises InjecAgent attack success on Llama 3.1 8B (0.862 to 0.922)

report: PIPETTE is trained on AgentDyn and evaluated on AgentDojo and ASB; the static results are averages over five attack templates; Meta-SecAlign and SecOPD are evaluated only on the bases their authors released, so PIPETTE is compared with each on that base
results r_msa_*: Meta-SecAlign-8B is measured without its base model in the same protocol, so its results carry no comparison

results r_*: Table 2 gives only paired changes against the undefended baseline, pooled over five models; the defended results carry those changes and the undefended evaluations carry no value; Holm-corrected p-values are 0.10 or above for every attack-success change

evaluations ev_*: Stage 2 training data tags only the inserted probe as Ring 3 inside a Ring 2 context (Step 4, p. 9); the paper does not say how rings were assigned on the OOD test sets, so whether the injected span is given to the model at test time is not reported
results r_ad_*_neu: Table 6 prints NeuExe ASR 48.44 (no defence) and 1.56 (Provenance-Aware), while the text gives 47.81% and 0.87% (p. 12); the record codes the table
results r_ae_*: the win rate is measured against the undefended base model, so the undefended model has no value of its own and the only comparisons are Provenance-Aware against Baseline SFT

report: Table 1 values for RFT-gate, DPO-gate and the two controls are three-seed means, the rest single runs; training rollouts were collected in the attacked environment of the same benchmark, and DPO-gate lowers travel utility (33.3% to 16.7%, Table 2)
defences flags, iso: the poster names the prompt-stage defences but does not give their wording; what the context flags mark is not described
report: 20 queries per condition; the authors repeated the runs at temperature 0.7 and report 91 to 99% agreement per query, not separate numbers

defences raised_*: trains_carry_through is coded yes_exact_targets because the self-generated scenarios require acting on legitimate guidance in tool outputs and the targets are the frozen model's own clean-context predictions (pp. 1, 7)

report: the edits need white-box access to activations and directions estimated from labelled hijacked and resisted trajectories of the same suite; directions transfer poorly across channels, and attacks are not adaptive to the direction except in the paper's Appendix J

status: value found in the third reading
detail: r_sepatt_meta_R1 ('1.3', page 7, chart label)

status: value found in the third reading
detail: r_gk_none_general_utility ('67.4', page 7, chart label)

results with value_source figure_only: values are printed as bar labels inside Figures 3 and 4; value_source has no value for a printed chart label, so they are coded figure_only and the printed value is kept (checked against the page text by the batch notebook)

results r_alpaca_meta_general_utility, r_sepclean_meta_R2clean: Figure 4 prints 94.4 (Meta SecAlign, AlpacaEval2) and 96.1 (Meta SecAlign, SEP without attack) as bar labels, but in every text extraction each runs into the next label (94.496.8, 96.198.0), so the values cannot be checked against the page text; they are coded figure_only without a value, carry no comparison, and are listed here for a human check (p. 7)

claim k1: the abstract gives Meta SecAlign 56.4% utility and 74.4% ASR on CySE; Figure 4 prints 56.4 for Meta SecAlign's CySE utility but 7.3 for its CySE ASR, and 74.4 is the undefended Llama3 ASR on SEP (p. 7); the coded results follow the figure

defence reasalign_l, reasalign_q: preference optimisation trains the separate logic judge used in the test-time search, not the answering model; distillation because the reasoning targets were written by GPT-4o-mini

evaluations ev_*_none_*, ev_*_rv_*: Section 6.1 says the five attack categories (Naive, Completion, Multi-round, Ignore, Escape) were used to build RedVisor's training data and are the same five used in Table 3; Section 7.3 says the tested patterns were unseen in training, and Appendix E.1 says the payload is a random UUID unseen in training (pp. 6, 7, 19)

results r_util_*: Appendix D.2 says WinRate compares RedVisor's responses against the vanilla backbone, but Section 7.6 prints a win rate of 87.27% for the undefended Llama-3 backbone itself; the reference model of the win rate is not clear (pp. 8, 19)

defences reta_*: RETA's defender is trained by RL on attacks found beforehand by a trained attacker, not co-evolved online, so axis 2 is preference_optimisation (reward-based RL, as for VerIH) rather than adversarial_rl
defences spot_*: the paper describes Spotlighting as provenance-signalling transformations without naming the variant; coded delimiters_markers as in the other records
defence msa_q: the paper does not say how MetaSecAlign was obtained for Qwen3-4B (the released models are Llama-based); the base condition is matched_unstated
report: every undefended configuration is attacked successfully in 100% of cases because the injections were written to succeed; BPP is judged by another LLM relative to the undefended model's output

comparisons c_f4_*: Figure 4 is said to use the strongest attacker, but SafeReview's values there equal its Qwen3-4B row in Table 2, so the comparison uses that evaluation with the attacker marked matched_unstated; SecAlign's base and training data are not stated

report: attack success is not measured directly: FPR depends on a threshold calibrated per condition and the average rating mixes defence effect with review calibration; the GRPO attackers were trained against the undefended reviewer
results r_l_*_sep_util: SEP utility is not stated to be scored on clean or attacked inputs, so it stays quantity other and R2clean coverage unclear (a reading problem, not a schema gap)
defence msa_q: Meta-SecAlign is re-trained by the authors on Qwen3.6-27B with the same 19K Cleaned-Alpaca data as SecOPD, not the released checkpoint (p. 6)

defences secpo_*, atdpo_*: adversarial training is a per-step PAIR search against the current checkpoint, not a learned attacker; axis 2 has no value for search-based adversarial training, so it is recorded in the components
evaluations ev_q_*_adutil, ev_q_*_adasr: all AgentDojo numbers, including the undefended arm, are run with AgentDojo's repeat-user-prompt defence (following Meta-SecAlign)

claims k2: under the white-box Basic Adaptive attack (Table 18), SecPO with adversarial training (10.6%) is slightly above adversarial training with DPO (9.7%); white-box attacks are outside the paper's stated threat model
report: the utility judge for AlpacaEval2 and SEP is Claude-Opus-4.8 (Appendix B); the judge names are the paper's

claim k1: the 94.7% figure is for the full system, which includes input sanitisation; the in-scope comparison is the ablation without the sanitiser, whose attack success is only given pooled over all six categories, including direct injection

report: the base model is described only as a 7B pre-trained model and the training and test data as collected from operational environments; which model the Instruction Hierarchy prompt runs on is not stated and is taken to be the same base
evaluations ev_*_inline: there is no undefended arm: the reference is the harness's one-line inline instruction, so the comparison is between two prompting defences

report: the paper's main defence, plan-then-gate, sends unplanned state-changing calls to a separate checker and is left out as system-level; two identical undefended runs flipped 15% of attack outcomes, so differences under about 10 points are within noise, as the author notes

report: no utility of the distilled student is reported, so the security result cannot be weighed against task performance; the input layout is not described beyond the Llama-3.2 chat template, so axis 1 is coded no_signal
claims k1: against Completion and Ignore-Completion the student (4.81%, 3.85%) is well above the teacher (0.48%, 0.00%)

report: AFCR is the attack-success measure here (false closure of malicious alerts); Qwen 2.5 never escalates any alert (0% intervention, 0% action accuracy), so its AFCR is 100% under every condition and its comparisons are uninformative; decoding settings are not fully specified, as the paper states

report: the paper does not name the model behind the Baseline and Spotlighting-Only arms or which spotlighting encoding they use (delimiters or Base64); its headline result (36.0% to 17.2%) is for the full layered system, which is out of scope; no claim is coded for the spotlighting arm alone
report: distractors are plausible irrelevant instructions rather than attacks, so distractor execution is coded as a proxy for injection success; the GPT-5.4 mini defence rows are single runs

report: a re-measurement of rendering untrusted text as images (the Pictionary idea) across six multimodal models; the Haiku 5.5 row is a closed model named as printed; the paper's figures show that larger fonts, higher resolution and a search over eight fixed candidates remove much of the protection
evaluations ev_*_sp_*: Table 3 uses a separate-page protocol (commands on their own page with a question-referencing lead-in) on 90 sources, so it is not comparable with Table 1's inline protocol

results r_* (R1): ASR is a conditional answer flip on GSM8K pooled over three payload families (reasoning rewrite, false verified answer, explicit instruction); it does not check that an injected instruction was carried out, so R1 is coded as a proxy

evaluations ev_base3_rag, ev_rag3_rag: the base RAG ASR is 65.5 in Tables 1, 3, 7 and 8 but 65.6 (99/151) in Table 5, whose caption notes reporting-granularity differences; the TRACER RAG denominator is 164 in Table 5 and 160 for the held-out and defence-aware runs
claims k2: the 78 to 82% clean accuracy is a range read from Figure 4 and the text; no exact clean accuracy is given for the RAG checkpoint

claims k3: the 13.9% 3B average appears only in the text; it equals the mean of the four Table 8 values for the multi-framing model; the 7B 9.4% is the epoch-1 checkpoint, the final 7B checkpoint averages 10.8%
defences t6: the paper does not say which TRACER checkpoint was used for the mixed-evidence test (Table 6), and gives no base evidence accuracy

report: same authors as the defence-backfire study (zenodo.20735483) with overlapping models, suites and defences; the AgentDojo cells here differ from that report's (Llama Scout banking undefended 30.6 against 31.9), so they are separate runs; the two Claude models are near zero on AgentDojo throughout; model names are as printed

report: the steering matrices are trained on trust conversations without injections and applied to both user turns and tool outputs; steering only the user turns raises attack success for both Qwen models (Appendix D.7), so the effect comes from the tool-output positions

report: the paper's own defences always include tool filtering (ATF) or toolset restoration (NTR); the only in-scope comparison is ASB's delimiter defence against no defence; GPT-4's attack success rises under delimiters (0.4456 to 0.5619)

report: the paper's main subject (deterministic monitors, human approval, taint tracking) is system-level and the D3 stack contains an LLM detector; both are left out under the review's scope rules, and most of the paper's results come from a simulation with an assumed model
evaluations ev_15_*_lvl*: Table 13 counts were reconstructed from printed rates; the raw sample log was not kept (p. 13); at levels 4 and 5 only half the outputs parse as tool calls
evaluations ev_*_att: attack episodes pool the static attack families; the paper's persistence figures (Tables 17 and 18) compose per-task rates over k attempts rather than running repeated attacks
defences verih_*: VerIH trains with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards; axis 2 has no value for non-adversarial RL, so it is coded preference_optimisation
comparisons c_*_ia: InjecAgent attack success is computed on each condition's valid replies, whose number changes with the lever (for example 81 to 93 of 300 for Qwen3-1.7B), so c3 is unmatched

report: the lever was chosen by search on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-1.7B and two other models; the paper's sealed overall verdict is NONE (two of six models), and held-out families mostly fail the random-direction control; the study is described by its author as AI-run, and its number rechecks name a commercial assistant

report: the injection test is one model in 4-bit (in bf16 the model ignores the injection at baseline) and is presented by the author as a replication of prior steering work, not a contribution; the exploratory random-direction check places the single control draw at the 91st percentile; the study is described as AI-run
